source.title: Scaling Laws for a Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Model

page_placements.theme: Task structure and metric choice determine additional scaling forms

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper measures test loss in an AlphaZero reinforcement-learning setting and reports that it does not follow a power law, challenging the extension of that form to other training regimes.
record.gate_note: Only the solver-labelled test-loss results directly test V5. The paper’s Elo-based parameter, compute, and compute-optimal-size results use playing strength rather than loss; they are recorded under fits_no_version. Language-model results mentioned from other papers are cited background, not this study’s results.
record.test_reason: The study moves scaling analysis to a new training regime: AlphaZero self-play RL on board games. Its only loss-based result bears on V5. Appendix F measures Connect Four test loss on a solver-labelled set and states that it does not scale as a power law. The main power-law results use Elo/playing strength, a different construct from loss, so they go under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors find that AlphaZero playing strength (Elo) scales as a power law in model size and compute on Connect Four and Pentago, with near-identical exponents. The derived optimal-size-versus-compute law fits their data. Large models are more sample efficient. AlphaZero and AlphaGo Zero appear undersized. Oware shows the same form but with training problems. Solver-labelled test loss is not a power law and is a poor indicator of performance scaling.
record.recipe_differences: Uses AlphaZero reinforcement learning on board games and Elo/playing strength for its main scaling analyses, rather than autoregressive language-model pretraining and held-out cross-entropy loss. Its test-loss analysis uses solver-labelled game states.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported scaling differs across games, especially Oware versus Connect Four and Pentago. The authors note that training length affects the size-scaling exponent, that Oware convergence issues affect its exponents, and that hyperparameter tuning could affect exponents; they leave the impact of hyperparameters for future work.

fits_no_version.finding: Elo-based playing strength scales as a power of parameter count: αN 0.88 for Connect Four, 0.87 for Pentago, 0.75 for Oware (Oware not converged).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In AlphaZero, playing strength follows a power law in network size when training is not compute-bottlenecked.

fits_no_version.finding: The Pareto-front playing strength scales with training compute: αC 0.55 for Connect Four and Pentago, 0.37 for Oware.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: AlphaZero playing strength follows a power of training compute for compute-optimal agents.

fits_no_version.finding: Elo-optimal parameter count scales with compute: exponents 0.62, 0.63 and 0.49, matching the prediction αC/αN.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The Elo-optimal AlphaZero model size grows as a power of compute, derivable from the size and compute exponents.

fits_no_version.finding: The fitted αN grows with training steps and converges by 10^4 steps (Fig. 9). In Oware it is still rising. Under fixed inference compute a smaller exponent appears (App. B).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Playing-strength size exponents depend on training length and on inference-compute constraints.

fits_no_version.finding: At equal data, larger models reach higher Elo (Fig. 5), but they need more data to reach the compute Pareto front (Fig. 4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger AlphaZero agents are more sample efficient.

record.problems: The test-loss evidence is presented in a figure without numerical values or stated uncertainty. The test set is specific to random Connect Four games annotated by a solver. Oware scaling is explicitly limited by failure of large models to converge and insufficient training time.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for individual model sizes or intermediate training-step curves were extracted; the paper reports their trends in figures, while the summarized scaling exponents and test-loss trends are captured above. Cited results from other papers were excluded.

untested.parts: Loss scaling is tested only for Connect Four, against model size only (not compute or data), on an off-distribution random-game test set. Pentago and Oware loss are not measured. Image/video, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer are not covered.
No loss extrapolation from small to large runs.
Optimal size versus compute is derived from Elo, not loss; no token allocation.
Depth is held at a fixed MLP shape; no shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
No downstream-versus-loss or language-model downstream analysis.
Hyperparameter and fitting-choice effects on loss exponents are not tested.

record.verdict_notes: The tranche changed from T5 to T3: the study is a new-setting test, not a dedicated argument against a version. The loss result rests on one figure for one game, on an off-distribution random-move test set, with no numbers or uncertainty. The V5 verdict should therefore be read as narrow. A reader treating 'power-law form' as covering any performance metric would read r3–r11 as supporting V5 for RL. They are kept off V5 here because V5 refers to the loss law.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test held-out language-model pretraining loss against parameters, tokens, or compute.
It does not fit loss laws on small runs and evaluate predictions on much larger runs.
It derives and evaluates compute-optimal model size using Elo/playing strength, not loss; it does not test token allocation.
The study does not compare architecture shapes at fixed parameter count.

The test is limited to AlphaZero on Connect Four, using solver-labelled game states; it does not test image or video models, repeated data, fine-tuning, transfer, or other reinforcement-learning settings.
Playing strength is evaluated, but the study does not test downstream-task performance as a function of pretraining loss or language-model scale.

The study notes possible hyperparameter effects and differing exponents across games, but does not systematically test fitting choices or the setup-dependence of language-model exponents and allocations.

relation.reason: Appendix F directly tests whether loss follows a power law with model size in self-play reinforcement learning.

tranche.reason: For V5, the directly relevant loss measurements explicitly fail power-law scaling or show only weak improvement. These results qualify or challenge the version; the main playing-strength laws measure a different quantity.

source_check.notes: Playing strength follows power laws while solver-labelled test loss does not. Numerical loss values are figure-only; the qualitative descriptions and 0.336 irreducible policy loss are stated in the text.

statements.correction: Oware: largest networks underperform smaller networks and fail to converge. Connect Four: solver-labelled random-move test states; value loss changes little and decreases then increases with size; test loss does not follow a power law. Checkers: no results reported.
statements.problem: Oware deterioration and Connect Four loss behavior are supported, but this study reports no Checkers results. Distribution shift is not directly assessed.

statements.correction: Connect Four αN=0.88 and Pentago αN=0.87: 10^4 optimization steps, treated as compute-unbottlenecked. Oware αN=0.75: insufficient training for convergence; exponent still increasing; largest models underperform.
statements.problem: All three exponents are correct, but the opening compute-unbottlenecked condition applies to Connect Four and Pentago, not the explicitly unconverged Oware runs.
